correctness.rationale: The known single-coordinate law normalizes each independent response to fα(x)=Cα(1−x²)^(α−1) on (−1,1), so the sum is an even, absolutely continuous convolution with no boundary mass. On (0,2), substituting x=s/2+(1−s/2)u separates the power (1−s/2)^(2α−1) and the positive quadratic B_u(s) in the proof. For α≤1/2 each kernel is strictly log-convex because log B_u is strictly concave and has exponent α−1<0, while the log of the power contributes convexity; pointwise strictness and Hölder yield strictness for the integral. The two endpoint neighborhoods in the convolution contribute the stated s^(2α−1) divergence below threshold and logarithms at equality. At the outer edge the remaining fixed-domain integral has a finite positive limit, so the exponent 2α−1 gives all three boundary regimes. Divergence at both ends of the half-support and strict log-convexity give precisely one subcritical minimum. For 1/2≤α<1 the fixed-domain kernel is strictly decreasing; α=1 is triangular. For α>1, layer-cake overlap lengths are nonincreasing, and for any interior positive separation a positive-measure set of pairs of half-widths has |r−t|<s<r+t, giving strict decrease. For α>1/2, L² translation continuity gives a finite continuous center. The strictly negative critical log derivative at each fixed interior s and continuity in α put the subcritical minimizer to its right for α close to 1/2. Writing ε=2−s and δ=1−2α, the log derivative in ε is −δ/ε+(1−α)/(2−ε/2)+O(ε) uniformly near criticality, since the hypergeometric factor is analytic at an argument of order ε². Its zero gives δ/ε→1/4. The finite checker was inspected, not executed.
